scenes.name: The Velvet Underground y el Exploding Plastic Inevitable
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Lou Reed quería llevar al pop la mirada sin concesiones de Burroughs, Purdy y Selby (heroína, prostitución masculina, vida gay y travesti) y amaba el doo-wop, el R&B profundo y el «Sally Go Round the Roses» de las Jaynetts: para él la música era «la única cosa viva». John Cale venía del Dream Syndicate de La Monte Young, con sus drones meditativos; Reed ya había grabado una obra maestra del dron de una nota, «The Ostrich». Tocaban delante de películas en la Cinematheque de Jonas Mekas cuando Warhol los adoptó a finales de 1965 y Paul Morrissey les impuso como cantante a Nico, la «Pop Girl» de 1966. Su carta de presentación fue tocar ante 350 psiquiatras («un tratamiento de electroshock»); después vinieron Uptight y el Exploding Plastic Inevitable en el Dom de St Mark’s Place (abril): luces, estroboscopios, Screen Tests, bola de espejos, la danza sadomaso de Malanga y Woronov y drones a un volumen insoportable. En California chocaron con la escena local («ellos iban de ácido, nosotros de anfetamina»; Gleason los llamó camp y enfermos). Su primer single en Verve, de Tom Wilson, «All Tomorrow’s Parties» / «I’ll Be Your Mirror» (julio), un producto pop art total, no tuvo ni reseñas ni radio. Eran un espejo de la América de 1966 que casi nadie quiso mirar.

podcast.title: Breaking Gender Barriers – First Female Rock Drummer (Retrospectively)
podcast.body: When Maureen Tucker joined The Velvet Underground in 1965, there were no known women drummers in rock music; playing drums was widely considered a "man's job." She therefore broke significant gender barriers, though this pioneering role was largely unnoticed at the time, possibly due to her unconventional drumming setup. Only in retrospect has she received due recognition as a musical pioneer. "Mo broke down some serious gender barriers But oddly enough no one really took any notice at the time probably because she wasn't setting upper drums properly anyway So only in retrospect that Mo got her due as a musical pioneer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Inspiration for Style – Nigerian Drum Virtuoso
podcast.body: Maureen Tucker stated that her distinctive drumming style and setup, which included playing while standing and using felt mallets, were inspired by a Nigerian drum virtuoso. "Mo says her style and setup was inspired by a Nigerian drum virtuoso."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Joining The Velvet Underground
podcast.body: Moe Tucker joined The Velvet Underground at the age of 19, immediately picking up the sticks for the "weirdo New York band." Her decision to pursue music was driven by the appeal of playing in the band over her previous job as a keypunch operator at IBM. "She didn't pick up the sticks until she was 19 and immediately joined the Vellvets. Playing in this weirdo New York band sounded way more fun than being a key punch operator at IBM."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Joining The Velvet Underground – Unique Circumstances
podcast.body: Maureen Tucker was the last member to join The Velvet Underground. She was drafted into the band after their initial drummer quit and relocated to Nepal, where he later died of malnutrition. "She was drafted after the velvet's first drummer quit and moved to Nepal Where he would eventually die of male nutrition, but that's another story."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Radical Female Drummer Style
podcast.body: Mo Tucker was noted as a radical female drummer. Instead of sitting behind a standard drum kit, she played standing up, with bass drums turned on their sides, and used mallets instead of traditional drumsticks to strike everything. "Yeah, a woman drummer. That was radical and she played like a radical."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Unconventional Drumming Style
podcast.body: Moe Tucker, the original drummer for The Velvet Underground, developed a distinctive and unconventional drumming style. She played standing up, primarily used mallets instead of sticks, and notably played a bass drum positioned on its side, employing marching band drums or a timpani. Her approach focused on keeping time and providing deep rhythmic backing, which was visually striking and subtle yet mesmerizing on recordings. "Mot wasn't exactly what you would call a conventional rock drummer. First of all, she played standing up. She played mostly with mallets, not sticks. There was a snare drum and a couple of tom-toms, but no symbols. And most striking of all, her bass drum was on its side."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Unorthodox Drumming Style – Standing and Mallets
podcast.body: Maureen Tucker, often known as Mo, had an "unorthodox" drumming style and setup. Instead of sitting behind a conventional drum kit, she stood up to play. She used felt mallets instead of traditional sticks and laid her bass drum on its side to play it with mallets, similar to a marching bass drum. She also "hardly used symbols." "Most style was On orthodox instead of sitting down behind a conventional kit she stood up and played everything with felt mallets instead of sticks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pioneering Alternative Band – Female Drummer
xref.body: The Velvet Underground is widely considered by many to be the first true alternative band. Notably, with Maureen Tucker joining in 1965, they may also have been the first rock band of any kind to feature a female drummer. "our group considered by many to be the first true alternative band."
